This sample on the information spheredevelopment

Drag to turn. Each point of light is a site of the genome, placed by how it behaves across IAM-Atlas v2.1's 79 healthy cell types.
How to use: drag the sphere to turn it. Click a family below to show it alone (the sphere turns to face it); click it again, or Show every family, to bring all back. Choose one cell type to light only its sites. The slider sets how strongly a site must stand apart in one cell to be colored. Hover over a territory to read it.

What you are looking at

Every point of light is one site on the human genome, one of 191,458 that IAM-Atlas v2.1 measured in all 79 of its healthy cell types and that vary between them. The address globes place each site by where it sits on the DNA. This sphere places each site by how it behaves: its methylation in the 79 cell types. Sites that behave alike land near each other, wherever they sit in the genome.

Nobody placed these sites. The math did.

No person and no program chose where any site, cell or tissue goes. Each site's position is computed from its 79 measured levels alone, in four fixed steps, and the same steps are applied to every site:

  1. Each site becomes a point on a sphere. A site's level in a cell type is a probability b (methylated or not). Taking the square roots of b and 1−b in every cell type gives a vector whose length is always exactly one, because b + (1−b) = 1. Every site therefore lies on the surface of a sphere. The sphere is not a drawing choice; it is where probabilities naturally live.
  2. The site's own level is taken out. Without this step, a site's average level would decide where it lands, and mostly-methylated sites would simply crowd together. With it, a site is placed only by how it departs from its own level across the cells: which cells it is higher in, and which lower.
  3. The three directions along which sites differ most are kept. They hold 39 % of the differences between sites; the rest are not drawn.
  4. The positions are fixed. Every sample is later read on this same sphere.

Only then are the colors added. Each site is labeled with the cell type where it departs most from its own level, and the 79 cell types are grouped into 15 families by tissue and lineage. That labeling is ours; the positions are not. The labels were laid on top of positions already computed, and nothing in the computation knew which cells are related.

So what the picture shows is a finding, not a design. The blood lineages ended up side by side: bone-marrow progenitors, B and NK cells, T cells and myeloid cells. Gut, pancreas, lung and airway, kidney, brain and muscle each hold their own region. The methylation alone put cells that share a developmental origin, and so share regulatory programs, next to each other. A further pattern the geometry produced on its own: each cell's methylated sites and its unmethylated sites gather on opposite sides of the sphere (for T cells, each side tightly at 0.88 and 0.86 on a scale where 1 is all in one place), because taking each site's level out turns "higher in this cell" and "lower in this cell" into opposite directions.

How to read it

  • Territories (the colored glow) are where one family's identity sites are over-represented: its share of the sites there divided by its share of all identity sites, so a large family does not color the sphere by size alone. The dark lanes are where two families are nearly equal. Point at the sphere to read whose territory you are over and by how much.
  • Colored points are sites that stand apart in one cell type clearly, by at least 0.10 more than in any other: 41,241 of the 191,458. The rest carry no clear single-cell identity and are drawn as faint dust when "Every site" is on.
  • The dark sky (45 % of the sphere) holds no sites. It is masked, as cosmologists mask our galaxy on the microwave sky, rather than stretched to fill the sphere, because stretching would falsify the distances.

Why this geometry

The angle between two sites on this sphere is the Fisher–Rao distance of information geometry. For nearby states it is, up to a constant, the relative entropy between them: the same quantity IAM measures as disorder against a physical floor. The instruments and this sphere measure in one currency. The square-root geometry itself is decades-old mathematics, used for distances between probability distributions and between populations. What is new here is treating it as a sky: a masked spherical map of a whole methylome, read with the microwave-sky tools, with one individual compared against itself.

The two spheres

Address globeInformation sphere
A site's place is set bywhere it sits on the DNAhow it behaves across the 79 cell types
Neighbors aresites next to each other on a chromosomesites that act alike, wherever they are
It answerswhere on the genome a change iswhat kind of change it is, and in which cell's program
It cannot tellthat distant sites belong to one programwhere on a chromosome a change is

A loss along one stretch of chromosome 2 is one patch on the address globe and scattered points here. A cell's whole program failing at sites spread over every chromosome is scattered dots on the address globe and one territory here. The two are kept together because each sees what the other cannot.

Reading one sample

A sample is read against its own expected healthy self: the atlas mixed at the cell shares the IAM-Deconvolver found in that sample, with no other person's sample involved. Each site's change is measured in that site's healthy width and in the sample's own spread, exactly as the address globe reads it. A territory has changed when its mean change stands beyond the line pure chance crosses less than once in 20 samples, judged against the sample's own other territories. The number of changed territories is fixed by the measurement; the slider only fades everything else to dark so the change stands alone. The sample's distance from its own expected healthy self is given as a Fisher–Rao angle.

Status

Development, not commissioned. On the atlas's real healthy cells, 11 of 12 groups of cell-marking sites land together beyond what their methylation level alone would give, and look-alike groups with the same levels do not (0 of 100). The sample reading is next tested on planted changes, then on healthy bloods, which should stay dark.
